title: Gravitation
textbookText: Chapter 7 Gravitation Numerous theories of gravitation emerged in ancient Greek philosophy and were further elaborated upon through the Middle Ages by scientists from various parts of the world. These ideas gained significant momentum during the Renaissance and Scientific Revolution, ultimately culminating in the formulation of Newton's law of gravity. Sir Isaac Newton discovered the existence of gravity. It is said that he realised about gravity when he saw an apple fall down from a tree. Newton came up with the idea that some unseen force must attract the apple towards the Earth. He named this force “gravity” from the Latin word “gravitas”, meaning “weight”. Finally in series of his work, Newton came to establish a famous law of gravitation, now called as Newton’s universal law of gravitation and it is his most renowned work.

Newton’s law of gravitation 7.1 Introduction: Before understanding the insight of the chapter, let’s observe an activity. Observe the following phenomena. i) The Earth is holding itself and rotating while the atmosphere surrounds it. ii) Binding the Earth and the other planets, along with the perennial source of energy, the sun forms a solar system. iii) Binding the stars together giving rise to galaxies. iv) The constant motion of the heavenly bodies throughout the time.

What will be the ultimate source to all these phenomena? The study of all observed phenomena implies that there is an interaction between any two heavenly bodies, characterized by the weakest force known as the gravitational force. If such a force acts on a body due to the Earth, it is called gravity; if it acts between any two bodies, it is referred to as gravitation. Gravity always refers to gravitation, but gravitation may or may not refer to gravity.
